title: Test-time compute: a history from chess clocks to reasoning tokens
summary: How machines learned to trade thinking time for strength: from the first chess time limits and Shannon's sixteen-minute move, through iterative deepening, rollouts, and AlphaGo Zero's search, to chain of thought, o1, and Opus 5.5's always-on adaptive thinking, and the question of who now sets the clock.

topics: deep dive: a history of test-time compute, from chess clocks to reasoning tokens
concepts_taught: test-time compute as a budget allocated inside a fixed total: the chess clock turned thinking time from a courtesy into a resource, and every later system is an answer to who allocates it and who sets the total
iterative deepening and engine time management: anytime search that always has a move ready, with per-move allocation adjusted by best-move stability, easy moves, and soft/hard time bounds

search as policy improvement: rollouts and Monte Carlo tree search use a base policy at decision time to pick better than that policy would, and the improved choices become training targets (AlphaGo Zero)

the train-time/test-time compute exchange rate: Jones's Hex result (10x training eliminates about 15x test-time search) and Snell's difficulty-dependent compute-optimal allocation, with pretraining still winning on the hardest problems

reasoning tokens as the language-model ply: chain of thought buys extra forward passes, reinforcement learning teaches the model to spend them, and budget forcing or adaptive effort decide who holds the clock

lore.note: Alan developed his February 2024 'progress is flattening' admission without claiming a change of mind: he says he was watching one clock (training compute) and missed the second axis (test-time compute) that anyone who had studied chess engines would have watched. Per his write-the-falsifier practice, he stated one on air: if thinking-time gains stall where pretraining gains stall, the second axis was a detour, not a new road — and promised to say so if it happens.
